text: Why is an interpreter built from two mutually recursive functions, `eval` and `apply`, rather than one?
choices: `eval` handles the global environment and `apply` handles local ones, which cannot share a function.
Java forbids a method from recursing on two different parameter types, so the work must be split.
An expression is syntax and needs case analysis; a procedure is a value and needs none, so the two halves change for different reasons.
`apply` runs at compile time and `eval` runs at run time, so they belong to different phases.
explanation: Adding a new expression form — a conditional, a comparison — adds a case to `eval` and touches nothing else. Adding a new calling mechanism — closures, tail calls — changes `apply` and touches no expression case. The separation is why an interpreter can be extended repeatedly without becoming tangled, and Section 25.2 extends it three times.
